content: Asthma is the most prevalent chronic disease in children and remains highly prevalent in adults, imposing a significant burden on healthcare systems. Effective management of asthma is crucial to reduce disease-related complications and optimize the use of healthcare resources. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of asthma care led by specialized nursing professionals, such as asthma nurses, nurse practitioners, or physician assistants, who work relatively independently of physicians. This was compared to traditional physician-led asthma care. The scope of the review included outpatient asthma care in both primary care and hospital settings. A comprehensive search of databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, was conducted to identify relevant trials up to August 2012. Additional trials were identified through bibliographic searches and manual reviews of relevant publications. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials that compared nurse-led care to physician-led care for the same aspects of asthma management. The review included five studies involving a total of 588 participants, both adults and children. One study focused on 154 patients with uncontrolled asthma, while the remaining four studies included 434 patients with controlled or partially controlled asthma. The methodological quality of the studies was deemed good, although blinding of participants and providers to the intervention group was not feasible. The results showed no statistically significant differences between nurse-led and physician-led care in terms of asthma exacerbations or asthma severity after treatment. The follow-up periods in the studies ranged from six months to two years. Only one study assessed healthcare costs as an outcome, and no significant differences were observed. Quality of life, although not a primary outcome, was reported in three trials involving 380 participants. There was no statistically significant difference in quality of life between the two groups (standardized mean difference -0.03; 95% confidence interval -0.23 to 0.17). The authors concluded that there is no significant difference in outcomes between nurse-led and physician-led asthma care based on the available evidence. Nurse-led care may be a suitable option for patients with well-controlled asthma. However, the relatively small number of studies included in this review highlights the need for further research in diverse settings and among patients with varying levels of asthma control. Future studies should also include data on adverse events and healthcare costs to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of nurse-led asthma care.
